entries.title: Capitals Beat Sabres in Overtime, 4-3
entries.summary: Alex Tuch scored two goals, including the winner in overtime, against his former team on Saturday night.
entries.content:
Alex Tuch scored two goals, including the winner in overtime, to lead the Washington Capitals to a win over the Buffalo Sabres, 4-3 on Saturday night.

Charlie Lindgren made 18 saves for the Capitals.

Tuch opened the scoring for Washington when a pass bounced off Tage Thompson’s stick and into his own net. Dylan Strome scored 2:59 into the second period, then once more with 2:36 left in the period.

Tuch was acquired this summer by the Capitals from the Sabres via sign-and-trade. He signed an eight-year, $84 million deal to help bolster the Capitals’ offense.

Jack Quinn and Josh Doan scored early for Buffalo to put the visitors up by two. The Capitals’ offense found its footing, though, and turned up the pressure on the Sabres’ defense to gain the lead in the second period, only to have Noah Ostlund tie it once again 2:20 into the third period. The game remained tied through the remainder of the third period, despite multiple power play opportunities and scoring chances for both teams.

Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen made 30 saves for the Sabres.

The Capitals were coming off a loss to the previously winless Los Angeles Kings on Tuesday. And, after a three-day break which allowed them to get both Pierre Luc-Dubois and Justin Sourdif back into the forward lines, the looked far more complete against the Sabres.

Buffalo has now lost three games in a row and has just three points in its last five games.

Up Next

Sabres: At the San Jose Sharks on Tuesday

Capitals: Host the Philadelphia Flyers on Wednesday.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Republicans May Be Neglecting Their Most Reliable Voters
entries.summary: Evangelical Christians say they feel overlooked as Trump and his allies reach out to other groups, leading some to worry turnout could be a problem.
entries.content:
Two years into a Trump administration that social conservatives hoped would bring significant victories on abortion and other evangelical Christian voters’ priorities, some are unimpressed by what the president has delivered. The lack of enthusiasm has been exacerbated by a national campaign outreach strategy that seems to be targeting everybody but them.

The bottom line? Evangelical Christians feel overlooked.

The discontent among the Republican Party’s most loyal voting bloc raises an uncomfortable question ahead of Election Day: Will evangelicals remain faithful to show up when their party needs them?

“There's a lot of people who feel like this administration has got deaf ears to their social conservative concerns,” said one conservative operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to speak candidly.

Republicans concerned about evangelical turnout pointed to the cumulative effect of an administration that they said has downplayed social conservative priorities, such as anti-abortion measures, and enacted policies that made some evangelicals uncomfortable — particularly its combative approach to immigration.

Party strategists warn that — coupled with concerns from most voters about the rising costs of gas and groceries, worries of government corruption, and dissatisfaction with the Iran war — could be a recipe for disaster.

“When evangelical voters make up a substantial chunk of that base, and they’re not overly enthusiastic, they’re not excited, they’re frustrated, they don’t necessarily feel like they got what they asked for,” said Cole Muzio, a Republican operative who focuses on Christian outreach. “That tends to affect enthusiasm and participation.”

Unlike recent election cycles, abortion issues have played less of a central role in campaign messaging — candidates instead have focused on affordability issues. But even before campaigning began in earnest, anti-abortion activists felt betrayed by the administration's ambivalence. The Health and Human Services Department hasn’t sought to restrict access to abortion pills — and even approved a new, generic version of mifepristone — while activists remain skeptical of some HHS officials’ anti-abortion bona fides.

Some had also hoped that the Justice Department would enforce a nationwide abortion ban through the Comstock Act. It hasn’t happened.

The issue has been historically important to evangelicals. The Public Religion Research Institute found in a survey conducted just after the Supreme Court handed down its landmark abortion decision in 2022 that 37% of evangelical voters would only cast ballots for candidates who share their views on abortion.

“If you are a single-issue voter,” the conservative operative said, “you might just sit out” this election.

Another sore spot for evangelical voters has been the administration’s use of family separation and the killings of American citizens by immigration officers. Walter Kim, the president of the National Association of Evangelical Voters, said candidates must balance promoting immigration enforcement and family values to appeal to evangelicals.

“If a candidate could advocate for … strong borders,” Kim said, “while simultaneously recognizing, no, evangelicals strongly do not want family separation.”

He added that many candidates are missing the nuance on these issues, and some mistakenly view the community as a monolith or a “caricature” despite the bloc’s diversity of views.

“Evangelicals are looking for candidates who are able to hold a bit more complexity and engagement with the evangelical community,” Kim said.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement to The Washington Sun that the Trump administration has delivered on the president’s promises.

“President Trump is the ultimate turnout driver for the MAGA base,” Bis said. “He promised to secure our border, remove criminal illegal aliens from American communities, restore religious liberty, and reverse the disastrous policies of the previous administration.”

The White House released last month a list of what Trump has done for religious Americans, including creating the White House Faith Office and Centers for Faith in federal agencies, as well as establishing the Religious Liberty Commission.

Operatives who work to activate conservative Christian voters described a nationalized campaign environment in which the races are a referendum on the White House and the spending is being decided in Washington.

Multiple operatives who spoke with The Sun said that they anticipated evangelical turnout to be on par with previous midterm elections. Some of them, though, said even the most reliable voters say the party’s broader campaign strategy has failed to reach social conservatives effectively.

“I think they nod toward it,” said Chad Connelly, founder of Faith Wins, a Christian political group. “But how much do you think any campaign spends on turning out the evangelical vote?”

“They do the TV ads and the digital ads,” Connelly added. But he said it isn’t authentic outreach, where they “speak the evangelical language.”

Some operatives and activists disputed that more evangelicals could stay home than in a typical midterm. Eric Teetsel, the CEO and publisher of Chronicles Magazine, said there was no particular reason to expect evangelical voting to have a greater downturn than other groups this year.

“To the extent evangelicals don’t turn out, it will be because of the same reasons all other GOP voters don’t turn out,” Teetsel said.

Ralph Reed, founder of the Faith and Freedom Coalition, told The Sun that he doesn’t see evidence of the administration’s posture on abortion suppressing turnout, though he wished they would be more demonstrably pro-life on the campaign trail.

“I am a little concerned that I think the Republican Party writ large have been fearful of the life issue after the Dobbs decision and the 2022 and 2024 elections,” Reed said. “They are a little bit gun-shy about ever bringing up the life issue, and I think that’s a mistake.”

Money from cash-rich establishment groups affiliated with President Donald Trump and Republican congressional leaders has formed the spine of the Republican campaign. But some outreach efforts and ads — paid for and directed by party leadership — have struggled to connect with the priorities of evangelicals.

When asked for comment, the Republican National Committee directed The Sun to Lorenzo Sewell, the senior pastor at 180 Church in Detroit. Sewell welcomed Trump to his church during the 2024 presidential campaign, and he spoke at the Republican National Convention and prayed at Trump’s second inauguration.

Sewell told The Sun that any frustration from evangelicals is rooted in frustration with the media and polling, not with the president. He said that frustration wouldn’t keep them from voting.

“There is no pastor that has more influence than me,” Sewell said, noting that the increased influence was because of Trump.

Sewell said there has been grassroots action among faith leaders, including a gathering of about 150 of them along with developers this month in Grand Rapids, Michigan, to push for economic opportunity zones. “We’re seeing momentum,” he said.

For any evangelical considering sitting out this election, Sewell had a message: Staying home would reinforce a narrative that evangelicals don’t vote well in the midterms.

“You’re expecting the president to do something when Christians don’t even vote,” Sewell said, referring to disappointment from evangelicals that Trump didn’t push for an abortion ban. “Muslims vote more than Christians.”

Muzio said that beyond the scattered messaging that some evangelicals say misses the mark on their priorities, having the messaging come from outside groups that some voters perceived as inauthentic hasn’t helped.

“The messaging nationally sucks,” Muzio said. “A lot of these national groups, it’s so astroturf and it’s so negative, nasty or unreal.”

He used the Texas Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton as an example, noting Paxton’s history of corruption allegations and his wife filing for divorce last year “on biblical grounds.”

“You can be sold on, ‘Hey, this is the choice, and in order to best reflect your values in D.C., this is the best choice to make,’” Muzio said of Paxton. “But you can’t be sold the person.”

Trump made his pitch to evangelicals during his Kansas rally on Monday by relaying an apparent conversation with a Dallas-area pastor. Trump said the pastor had believed Trump was going to lead Christians to a period of prosperity in the faith that “nobody else can do.”

“And he turned out to be right,” Trump told the crowd.
entries.author: Ben T.N. Mause, Andrea Padilla

entries.title: Wizards Hold Off Bulls for a 124-120 Road Victory
entries.summary: Trae Young had 25 points and nine assists, and Kyshawn George added 22 points and nine rebounds.
entries.content:
CHICAGO — Trae Young had 25 points and nine assists, and the Washington Wizards held off the Chicago Bulls for a 124-120 victory on Saturday night.

Kyshawn George had 22 points and nine rebounds for Washington in the opener of a three-game trip. Anthony Davis added 19 points, and Justin Champagnie had 11 points and 14 rebounds.

The Wizards played without AJ Dybantsa, the No. 1 pick in the draft. The 19-year-old Dybantsa is day to day with a sprained left ankle, delaying his anticipated NBA debut.

Caleb Wilson had 30 points and 14 rebounds for Chicago in its home opener. It was the first double-double for the No. 4 selection in the draft, but he went 1 for 9 from 3-point range.

Forwards Noa Essengue and Patrick Williams were sidelined for Chicago, which was coming off a 132-125 win at Milwaukee on Friday. Essengue has a head contusion, and Williams is dealing with a groin injury.

The Bulls led by as many as 10 before they were outscored 40-20 in the third quarter. Young had seven points and five assists in the quarter, including a lob to Alex Sarr for a jam that gave the Wizards a 97-80 lead with 34 seconds remaining.

The Bulls went 12 for 43 from 3-point range. They are shooting 23% (28 for 124) from deep in three games this season.

Chicago opened a 60-50 lead on Wilson’s fast-break dunk with 2:02 left in the first half, punctuating a 10-0 run. He grabbed a rebound and scored on a reverse jam with 56 seconds remaining, but Washington’s Tre Johnson made a 3-pointer in the final seconds to make it 62-57 at the break.

Up Next

Wizards: At Charlotte on Monday night.

Bulls: At Boston on Monday night.

entries.title: Trump Calls Murkowski ‘Republicans’ Worst Senator’ Over Opposition to Elections Lawsuit
entries.summary: The Alaska senator publicly challenged the Trump administration’s lawsuit over certifying the results.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump lashed out at Sen. Lisa Murkowski for speaking out against his administration’s push to refuse to certify the election results unless Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan wins the race in Alaska.

“The Republicans’ Worst Senator, by far, Lisa Murkowski, of the Great State of Alaska,” Trump wrote late Saturday on Truth Social.

There are two Dan Sullivans running for Senate on Alaska’s ballot: incumbent Dan S. Sullivan and a retired schoolteacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., an independent candidate whom Republicans have accused of being in cahoots with Democrats to pull votes away from the sitting senator. Dan S. Sullivan is locked in a close race with Democratic nominee Mary Peltola.

Trump took credit for pushing the Justice Department to file a lawsuit on Thursday threatening state officials with legal repercussions unless Dan S. Sullivan wins reelection. Murkowski denounced the legal complaint, saying the DOJ “should never have filed this lawsuit.”

“Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot,” Murkowski wrote Friday on X.

Alaska’s ballot includes “(Registered Republican) Incumbent” after Dan S. Sullivan’s name and has no designation after Dan J. Sullivan. But Trump does not think that distinction makes things clear enough for voters, saying Democrats are “outright cheating” by allegedly putting Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot.

“At least let him use the name Senator Dan Sullivan as opposed to incumbent, because a lot of people don't know what incumbent means,” Trump told reporters Sunday.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and the Alaskans for Mary campaign filed a motion Friday to stop the Trump administration from blocking the election results.

On Sunday, Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the Justice Department’s lawsuit, even though Alaska’s state Supreme Court ruled in June that Daniel J. Sullivan could remain on the ballot.

“What's the crime? Well, it depends,” Blanche said Sunday on CNN’s “State of the Union.” “There could be a crime, but the real wrong here is that Alaskans are going to be confused and will not have their vote heard.”

Trump said Murkowski only won her election because of ranked-choice voting — which is a system that allows voters to rank their preferred candidates. If their vote cannot help their top choice win, their vote is applied to their second choice and so on.

“They’ve been trying to get rid of Lisa Murkowski forever in Alaska, then she came up with the Ranked Choice Voting SCAM, and pulled a nice hot iron out of the fire,” Trump wrote in another Truth Social post Saturday night. “Everyone thought she came in second or third, but then she ‘won.’ Miracles happen!”

Alaska has used ranked-choice voting since 2022, and Murkowski actually held a narrow lead over her opponents in the Senate election with 43% of the first choice votes before any ranking transfers had been made.

“The Ranked Choice Voting Ballot is a TOTAL DEMOCRAT SCAM meant to confuse the Voter, so that Senator Dan Sullivan will lose Votes to a man who has never participated in Politics before,” Trump wrote.

The president also encouraged Alaska to vote to repeal the voting system for state and federal elections through a ballot measure on Election Day.

Murkowski has broken with Trump several times since the start of his second term in office, sometimes serving as swing vote in the Senate for the president’s key policy goals. Last year, Murkowski voted against Pete Hegseth’s nomination for defense secretary and against Trump’s tariffs on Canada. The Alaska senator has also stood against Trump for renaming Mount Denali, the original name of her state's highest peak, Mount McKinley.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Alaska’s Peltola and Her Family Sustain ‘Minor Injuries’ in a Car Crash
entries.summary: The Democratic Senate candidate postponed the first two stops for her upcoming campaign blitz, citing the advice of medical professionals.
entries.content:
Former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee for Alaska, and her family sustained minor injuries after a car crash Saturday night, prompting her campaign to reschedule two of the eight stops for her upcoming “Alaska Always Tour.”

“Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits. Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover,” Cheryl Bruce, the campaign manager for Alaskans for Mary, wrote in a statement.

Another car struck the vehicle transporting Peltola and her family while they were en route to the Alaska Federation of Natives annual banquet, Bruce said.

“Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always Tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families,” Bruce added.

Peltola is running against two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in a race that recent polling suggests is highly competitive.

entries.title: Beatty Asks Judge to Compel Trump Administration to Disclose Emails and Texts about Kennedy Center Plans
entries.summary: A list of records suggests the president has been in “near-constant contact” with the center's management, Rep. Joyce Beatty's lawyers said.
entries.content:
By Michael Kunzelman

President Donald Trump's administration is withholding records documenting the scope of his influence over management of the Kennedy Center, according to attorneys for a Democratic lawmaker challenging the Republican president's plan to close the performing arts center for renovations.

A list of records in the Kennedy Center's possession suggests that Trump has been in “near-constant contact” with the center's management, either directly or through intermediaries, plaintiffs' lawyers said in a court filing on Sunday.

Attorneys for Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and ex officio member of the Kennedy Center board, are seeking a court order for the administration to turn over documents, emails and text messages that it has withheld based on its claims that they contain privileged presidential communications.

“These communications directly bear on the issues before the Court, and the claim of privilege cannot stand,” Beatty's lawyers wrote.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper didn't immediately rule on their request to compel disclosure of the records.

The list of withheld documents includes 19 text messages between Kennedy Center executive director and CEO Matt Floca and Trump executive assistant Natalie Harp regarding Kennedy Center-related matters. They exchanged 11 of those messages on Sept. 15, when the center's board voted for a third time to close the facility, according to Beatty's lawyers.

The list also includes approximately 180 center-related texts between Floca and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who was acting as Trump's “go-between,” Beatty's lawyers say. The plaintiffs' attorneys suspect the administration is engaging in impermissible "gamesmanship."

“Without access to these materials, (Beatty) will lack a complete picture of Defendants’ actions,” they wrote.

The White House didn't immediately comment on the court filing.

Cooper, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama, ruled in May that the Kennedy Center illegally added Trump’s name to the building and ordered it removed.

Trump, who was named the Kennedy Center’s chairman last year by loyalists on its board, has said the building is in dangerous condition that will require it to be “ripped down.” The board voted to close the center after Cooper blocked the institution from returning Trump’s name to the building.

On Sept. 16, Floca ordered a temporary closure of the center's main building. A day later, Cooper ordered the Kennedy Center to provide 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building.

entries.title: Trump Attacks El-Sayed As a ‘Jihadist’ in Anti-Muslim Screeds
entries.summary: The campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, called the rhetoric a “lie” and “bad faith attacks.”
entries.content:
President Donald Trump repeatedly called Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate from Michigan, a “jihadist” who should not be allowed in the halls of Congress unless he goes through metal detectors.

“I'm here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” Trump said at a rally Sunday in Lake Huron, Michigan — adding later that El-Sayed should not earn the Senate seat because “anyone with that record of support for jihadists would be screened and unable to get a seat on an airplane.”

If El-Sayed wins the Nov. 3 election against Republican Mike Rogers, he would be the first Muslim to serve in the Senate. Trump and his allies have repeatedly linked El-Sayed, without any evidence, to radical militant Islamic ideology while casting Rogers as “apple pie” and “perfect” for the state. El-Sayed, who was born in Michigan, has denounced the Muslim Brotherhood.

Rogers appeared to distance himself from Trump’s previous comments in an interview earlier Sunday after a back and forth with NBC’s Kristen Welker on “Meet the Press.”

“I’ve never called him a terrorist,” Rogers said after Welker asked if he agreed with Trump’s comments calling El-Sayed a “violent terrorist.”

Trump’s Michigan rally comes the day after former President Barack Obama campaigned alongside El-Sayed to shore up last-minute support for the Democrat ahead of the midterms.

El-Sayed’s campaign said the candidate would respond to the Trump comments during a campaign event later Sunday.

“While they lie and resort to desperate, bad faith attacks, Abdul remains laser focused on his plans to bring down costs and stand up to the chaos and corruption in Washington,” Cole Wozniak, El-Sayed’s campaign spokesperson, said in a statement following Trump’s rally. “Michigan knows Trump is on the ballot on November 3rd—and they will vote like it by rejecting Trump’s rubber stamp Mike Rogers and sending Abdul to the Senate.”

El-Sayed has explicitly pushed back on any attempts to tie him to the Muslim Brotherhood, a group founded in Egypt in 1928 which has been seen as a precursor to some prominent fundamentalist Islamic groups.

During the rally, Trump demanded that El-Sayed, if elected, go through security measures before entering the Capitol similar to those required by TSA at U.S. airports.

“He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate. I want him to have a metal detector,” Trump said. “If Abdul gets to the Senate, he would have access to our nation's most closely guarded national security secrets, and his vote would wield power over our military, our borders, our homeland security, and much more than that.”

Trump spoke alongside David Beamer, whose son Todd Beamer died on United Airlines Flight 93 during the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks after he and fellow passengers foiled part of the terror plot and forced the aircraft into the ground.

David Beamer, like Trump, made several comments attempting to tie El-Sayed and left-leaning Democrats to support to terrorism.

“What's different this time is the enemy has not come from abroad,” Beamer said. “The enemy is right here among us, local terrorists, local citizens that want to demolish our country. They call themselves Democratic Socialists of America."

El-Sayed has denied having any connection to DSA, telling The Wall Street Journal earlier this year that he is “not technically or practically” a part of the political group.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin
